Here, we show that an auxiliary word recognition model, which can be trained on unlabeled data, provides a strong defense.

Under this scheme, all inputs are classified by the composed model $C \circ W$ .

This modular approach, with $W$ and $C$ trained separately, offers several benefits: (i) we can deploy the same word recognition model for multiple downstream classification tasks/models; and (ii) we can train the word recognition

model with larger unlabeled corpora.

We discuss these aspects in detail below.

ScRNN with Backoff	We now describe semi-character RNNs for word recognition, explain their limitations, and suggest techniques to improve them.

Inspired by the psycholinguistic studies  ,  ,  proposed a semi-character based RNN (ScRNN) that processes a sentence of words with misspelled characters, predicting the correct words at each step.

ScRNN treats the first and the last characters individually, and is agnostic to the ordering of the internal characters.

At each sequence step, the training target is the correct corresponding word (output dimension equal to vocabulary size), and the model is optimized with cross-entropy loss.

While  demonstrate strong word recognition performance, a drawback of their evaluation setup is that they only attack and evaluate on the subset of words that are a part of their training vocabulary.

In principle, one can design models to predict (correctly) only a few chosen words, and ignore the remaining majority and still reach 100% accuracy.

Below, we explore different ways to back off when the ScRNN predicts UNK (a frequent outcome for rare and unseen words): Pass-through:

The spell-correction models are evaluated on their ability to correct misspellings.

The test setting consists of reviews where each word (with length $\ge 4$ , barring stopwords) is attacked by one of the attack types (from swap, add, drop and keyboard attacks).

In the all attack setting, we mix all attacks by randomly choosing one for each word.

This most closely resembles a real world attack setting.

We found ATD to be the best freely-available corrector.

For the ScRNN model, we use a single-layer Bi-LSTM with a hidden dimension size of 50.

For training these networks, we corrupt the movie reviews according to all attack types, i.e., applying one of the 4 attack types to each word, and trying to reconstruct the original words via cross entropy loss.

This is a $32\%$ relative error reduction compared to the vanilla ScRNN model with a pass-through backoff strategy.

Intuitively, one might suppose that word-piece and character-level models would be more robust to such attacks given they can make use of the remaining context.

However, we find that they are the more susceptible.
